sections.title: Learning Objectives
items: Explain how a buffer resists pH change and calculate buffer pH using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
Describe buffer capacity and what happens when acid or base exceeds buffer capacity
Predict whether aqueous solutions of salts are acidic, basic, or neutral
Interpret acid–base titration curves and locate the equivalence point and half-equivalence point
Choose an appropriate indicator for a given titration

sections.title: Concept 1 — Buffers and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation
body: A buffer is a solution containing appreciable amounts of a weak conjugate acid–base pair, such as CH3COOH and CH3COO−. It resists large pH changes when small amounts of acid or base are added.
The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation gives the pH of a buffer: pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]). When [A−] = [HA], pH = pKa.
Buffer capacity is the amount of acid or base a buffer can neutralize before the pH changes significantly. Capacity is greatest when [HA] and [A−] are both large and roughly equal.
Example buffer: a solution of acetic acid and sodium acetate (CH3COOH + CH3COONa). The initial pH of an equimolar buffer equals pKa of acetic acid, 4.74.

worked_example.question: A buffer contains 0.50 M CH3COOH and 0.50 M CH3COONa. Ka = 1.8 × 10−5. (a) What is the buffer pH? (b) What is the pH after 0.020 mol of HCl is added to 1.0 L of buffer?
worked_example.solution: (a) pKa = −log(1.8×10−5) = 4.74. pH = 4.74 + log(0.50/0.50) = 4.74. (b) Added H+ converts CH3COO− to CH3COOH: [CH3COO−] = 0.48 M, [CH3COOH] = 0.52 M. pH = 4.74 + log(0.48/0.52) = 4.71. pH changed by only 0.03 units — the buffer worked.

common_mistakes: Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for strong acid/base solutions (it only applies to buffers of weak conjugates).
Forgetting to use the NEW concentrations after acid/base is added — always do the stoichiometry first.

sections.title: Concept 2 — Hydrolysis of Salts: Acidic, Basic, or Neutral?
body: Salt ions can react with water (hydrolyze) and change solution pH. The conjugate of a weak acid (e.g., CH3COO−, CN−) is a weak base; the conjugate of a weak base (e.g., NH4+) is a weak acid.

Rules: (1) A cation that is the conjugate acid of a weak base → acidic (e.g., NH4+ in NH4Cl). (2) An anion that is the conjugate base of a weak acid → basic (e.g., CN− in KCN). (3) Ions of strong acids/bases (Cl−, Na+) are neutral spectators. (4) Small, highly charged metal cations (Al3+, Fe3+) make solutions acidic by binding water and releasing H+.
Example: NH4Br → NH4+ (weak acid, from NH3) + Br− (neutral, from HBr) → the solution is acidic. KNO2 → K+ (neutral) + NO2− (weak base, from HNO2) → the solution is basic.

worked_example.question: Predict whether aqueous solutions of the following salts are acidic, basic, or neutral: (a) Al(NO3)3 (b) RbI (c) KHCO2 (d) CH3NH3Br
worked_example.solution: (a) Al3+ hydrolyzes → acidic. (b) Rb+ and I− are neutral spectators → neutral. (c) HCO2− is the conjugate base of a weak acid → basic. (d) CH3NH3+ is the conjugate acid of a weak base → acidic.

common_mistakes: Assuming every salt is neutral — check each ion's parent acid/base.
Treating metal cations like Na+ the same as Al3+ (small highly charged cations are acidic).

sections.title: Concept 3 — Acid–Base Titrations and Titration Curves
body: A titration curve plots pH versus volume of added titrant. For a strong acid + strong base, pH jumps sharply near the equivalence point (pH ≈ 7). For a weak acid + strong base, the equivalence point is above pH 7; for a weak base + strong acid, it is below pH 7.
At the half-equivalence point, half the analyte has been neutralized: [HA] = [A−] and pH = pKa. This is the flattest part of the curve (maximum buffering).
Indicators are weak acids whose color depends on pH. Choose an indicator whose color-change range (pKa ± 1) brackets the equivalence-point pH.

worked_example.question: In the titration of 40 mL of 0.100 M CH3COOH (Ka = 1.8 × 10−5) with 0.100 M NaOH, predict the pH at: (a) 0 mL added (b) 20 mL added (c) 40 mL added.
worked_example.solution: (a) Initial weak acid: [H3O+] ≈ √(Ka·Ca) = √(1.8×10−5 × 0.100) = 1.3 × 10−3 M, pH = 2.87. (b) At 20 mL, half-equivalence: pH = pKa = 4.74. (c) At 40 mL, equivalence: all acetic acid converted to CH3COO− (0.050 M). Kb = Kw/Ka = 5.6×10−10; [OH−] = √(Kb·Cb) = √(5.6×10−10 × 0.050) = 5.3×10−6 M; pOH = 5.28, pH = 8.72.

common_mistakes: Assuming the equivalence-point pH is always 7 (true only for strong acid + strong base).
Using initial acid concentration instead of the diluted concentration after titrant is added.

items.q: A buffer is prepared from 0.200 M CH3COOH and 0.200 M CH3COONa (Ka = 1.8 × 10−5). What is its pH?
A buffer is prepared from equal volumes of 0.200 M CH3COOH and 0.600 M CH3COONa. (a) What is the pH? (b) Is the solution acidic or basic?
items.answer: (a) pH = 4.74 + log(0.600/0.200) = 4.74 + 0.48 = 5.22. (b) pH > 7? No — 5.22 < 7, so acidic (buffer of a weak acid, even with excess conjugate base).

items.q: What is the pH of a buffer containing 0.250 M NH3 and 0.350 M NH4Cl? Kb(NH3) = 1.8 × 10−5.
How much solid sodium acetate must be added to 0.300 L of 0.50 M CH3COOH to make a buffer with pH = 5.00? (Assume negligible volume change.)
What mass of NH4Cl must be added to 0.750 L of 0.100 M NH3 to give a buffer with pH = 9.26? (Assume negligible volume change.)
A buffer contains 0.40 M HF and 0.40 M NaF (Ka = 6.8 × 10−4). What is the pH after 0.010 mol of NaOH is added to 1.0 L of buffer?
items.answer: Initial pH = pKa = 3.17. Added OH− converts HF to F−: [HF] = 0.39 M, [F−] = 0.41 M. pH = 3.17 + log(0.41/0.39) = 3.17 + 0.02 = 3.19.

items.q: Determine whether aqueous solutions of these salts are acidic, basic, or neutral: (a) FeCl3 (b) K2CO3 (c) NH4Br (d) KClO4
items.answer: (a) acidic (Fe3+ hydrolyzes) (b) basic (CO32− is conjugate base of HCO3−/H2CO3) (c) acidic (NH4+) (d) neutral (K+ and ClO4− both neutral)

items.q: Determine whether aqueous solutions of these salts are acidic, basic, or neutral: (a) Al(NO3)3 (b) RbI (c) KHCO2 (d) CH3NH3Br
Write the hydrolysis equation for the acetate ion, CH3COO−, in water and identify the solution as acidic or basic.
items.answer: CH3COO−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ CH3COOH(aq) + OH−(aq). Produces OH− → basic solution.

items.q: Explain why the neutralization of a strong acid with a weak base gives a weakly acidic solution. Use NH3 + HCl as your example.
items.answer: The product salt NH4Cl contains NH4+, the conjugate acid of weak base NH3, which hydrolyzes to produce H3O+: NH4+(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ NH3(aq) + H3O+(aq). The excess H3O+ makes the solution weakly acidic.

items.q: Explain why the neutralization of a weak acid with a strong base gives a weakly basic solution. Use CH3COOH + NaOH as your example.
items.answer: The product salt NaCH3COO contains CH3COO−, the conjugate base of weak acid CH3COOH, which hydrolyzes to produce OH−: CH3COO−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ CH3COOH(aq) + OH−(aq). The excess OH− makes the solution weakly basic.

items.q: Explain how to choose an appropriate indicator for the titration of a weak base with a strong acid.
items.answer: Find the pH at the equivalence point (below 7 for a weak base + strong acid), then choose an indicator whose color-change range brackets that pH (e.g., methyl red, pH 4.4–6.2, for a weak base titrated with HCl).

items.q: Explain why an indicator changes color over a range of pH values rather than at a single pH.
items.answer: An indicator is a weak acid HIn whose color depends on the ratio [In−]/[HIn]. That ratio changes gradually with pH (Henderson–Hasselbalch), so the visible color shifts over roughly pKa ± 1 pH units.

items.q: For the titration of 40 mL of 0.100 M CH3COOH (Ka = 1.8 × 10−5) with 0.100 M NaOH, calculate the pH after 20 mL of NaOH has been added.
For the same titration (40 mL of 0.100 M CH3COOH with 0.100 M NaOH), calculate the pH after 40 mL of NaOH has been added.
For the titration of 40 mL of 0.100 M CH3COOH with 0.100 M NaOH, calculate the pH after 41 mL of NaOH has been added (excess strong base).

sections.title: Key Terms
items: buffer
A solution containing a weak conjugate acid–base pair that resists pH change
Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]) for buffer solutions
buffer capacity
The amount of acid or base a buffer can neutralize before pH changes significantly
hydrolysis
Reaction of a salt ion with water to produce H3O+ or OH−
equivalence point
The point in a titration at which the added titrant exactly neutralizes the analyte
half-equivalence point
The point at which half the analyte is neutralized; pH = pKa
indicator
A weak acid whose color changes over a pH range; used to detect the endpoint
titration curve
A plot of pH versus volume of added titrant
